blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 2:49pm

Counsel to the panel of prosecutors Atty. Lorna Kapunan on Thursday apologized to lead defense counsel Atty. Sheila Sison for calling her a bully, clarifying that it is the Vice President who is the "real bully."
"Hindi naman siya ang bully. Ang talagang bully is the Vice President. She is the real bully," Kapunan said in an online interview.

Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday defended Sison after Kapunan called the latter a bully and accused her of disrespecting the prosecution and the senator-judges after the defense described the impeachment proceedings as “persecution.”

“Lorna Kapunan calling a defense counsel a bully is like calling David the aggressor against Goliath. It is a convenient way to vilify the person defending against an overwhelming display of political power," Duterte said.
But Kapunan said it is the Vice President who is the aggressor and bully.

"Nakita naman natin sa statement niya, tinitira niya lahat (We have seen her statement, she's criticizing everybody). She's bullying the senator-judges. Calling the impeachment trial as political theater. She's bullying the prosecutors. She's bullying the House," the defense lawyer stated.
Kapunan said Duterte "has disrespected all the institutions. So I want to correct my statement. It is not Attorney Sheila who is the bully. It is the Vice President herself."
"Apologies to Atty. Sheila. They're just doing their job as lawyers," she added. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
articles.summary: EU leaders meeting in Brussels will examine measures to curb the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. But they will also be looking to further agreement on the next EU budget ahead of some major…

image.caption: The EU is holding a summit as the bloc faces rising economic challengesImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Union leaders are to meet in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.
The meeting is also likely to see some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.
On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.
Here are the main topics on the agenda:
Chinese competition in focus
The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.
The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.
The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.
Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.
Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.
The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.
Divisive EU budget
The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.
Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.
The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.
Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.
Ukraine support
The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.
He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.

European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.
Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.

articles.title: Ombudsman vows impartial probe on VP Sara's assets
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman on Thursday vowed to conduct impartial probe on the National Bureau of Investigation"s referral on alleged missing declarations of Vice President Sara Duterte in her…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 2:41pm

The Office of the Ombudsman on Thursday vowed to conduct an impartial probe on the National Bureau of Investigation’s referral on alleged missing declarations of Vice President Sara Duterte in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

“The Office of the Ombudsman confirms receipt of the referral from the NBI concerning the SALN of Vice President Duterte.The Office assures the public that the matter will be handled thoroughly, independently and without any political color,” the Ombudsman siad.

“The referral and its supporting documents will undergo an initial evaluation to determine the appropriate action, including whether further investigation is warranted, in accordance with established procedures and applicable laws,” the Ombudsman added.
On Tuesday, the NBI referred its fact-finding investigation report on Duterte’s SALN to the Ombudsman for evaluation and appropriate action.

“The Bureau refers the matter to your Office, as the constitutional body with primary jurisdiction over public corruption under Article XI of the 1987 Constitution and Section 15 (1) of Republic Act No. 6770. The NBI stands ready to provide further records and to present its agents as witnesses should your Office require them,” the letter to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla read.

Prosecution witness, Atty. Alex Cabrera, testified during Duterte's impeachment trial that she and her husband, based on their joint filed SALN among other financial records, amassed P817 million unexplained wealth at the minimum and P1.5 billion at the maximum.

Cabrera made the conclusion after reviewing the financial records of the Vice President and her husband which include: SALNs, bank transaction and bank deposit records, insurance payment records, income tax returns and corporate records of the busines interests of the Duterte-Carpio couple.
Defense team lead counsel Sheila Sison said Cabrera’s testimony should not be given weight since they were mere “unbridled and erroneous conclusions of law and fact.” —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Doctors treating Elizabeth Struhs recommended involuntary mental health assessment of her mother, coroner hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into death of Queensland girl denied insulin by her religious parents is told Kerrie Struhs believed God would heal her daughter

  • Get our

blocks.text: Doctors were so concerned about the religious beliefs of Elizabeth Struhs’ mother they recommended she be subjected to an involuntary mental health assessment because she delusionally believed her daughter would be healed from type 1 diabetes, a coroner has heard.
Child safety officers, nonetheless, decided to return the eight-year-old home to live with her mother, Kerrie Struhs, over the objections of Brisbane-based doctors, in 2019.

Elizabeth died on 7 January 2022, at her home in Rangeville, Toowoomba, after her insulin was stopped by her father, Jason Struhs. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.
The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence from three child safety officers involved in Elizabeth’s case on Thursday.

Elizabeth came to the attention of the department of child safety in 2019 after she was hospitalised with late-stage diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July, a potentially fatal ailment that affects people with type 1 diabetes who are not given insulin. The court has heard she was so unwell she was in a coma and nearly died.
Despite her poor condition, Kerrie objected to Jason driving her to hospital, believing Elizabeth would be miraculously healed.
Kerrie later participated in an interview involving child safety officers and health staff.
Contemporaneous notes taken from the meeting presented in court read: “Kerrie stated that Elizabeth cannot keep this disease and she will be healed.
“(A health) consultant stated that they have treated 100s of children and parents and no one has ever reverted back from the diabetes or got rid of type 1,” the notes read.
“Kerrie stated that she has to trust in God to heal Elizabeth as God promised her he will hear her.”
A consultant asked Kerrie what she would do if she was home with Elizabeth and her sugar levels dropped, a sign of health risk.
“Kerrie stated that she will pray straight away,” the notes read.

The coroner has heard that doctors based in Brisbane repeatedly urged child safety officers not to return her home due to her religious beliefs, which they deemed “delusional”, but one told the court on Monday she felt “stonewalled” by them.
Notes of a phone call she made at the time were presented in court on Thursday.
“Child safety officer explained that the mother would not engage in any mental health assessments if recommended given her beliefs,” a child safety officer told her.
after newsletter promotion
“(The doctor) stated that this is why they believe she requires an involuntary assessment and that child safety could arrange this.”
Both parents were later convicted of failing to provide the necessities of life as a result of delaying seeking medical help during the incident, with Kerrie jailed.
Child safety officers decided to return her home into the care of her father, which they did in August.

They developed a safety plan for Elizabeth and had her parents sign an intervention with parental agreement – a form of voluntary arrangement to keep a child safe at home without needing a court-ordered custody or guardianship arrangement.
The document, which was presented in court, laid out the expectations the department had for Elizabeth’s parents.

It said child safety was “worried” that Kerrie and her other children would convince Elizabeth that she was “healed by God … which could lead to Elizabeth refusing to take her medication making her very sick or putting her at risk of death”.
Jason promised to provide insulin to his daughter and did so for two years, before he was convinced to stop by other members of the sect – known as the Saints – in 2021.
All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte keeps majority trust ratings amid impeachment trial
articles.summary: So far, the surveys show that public trust in and approval of Duterte have defied expectations of a reputation-bruising trial, where allegations of Duterte's unexplained wealth and wanton use of…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 2:10pm

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte continues to enjoy majority trust and approval ratings, according to two different surveys released this week, even as the Senate impeachment trial is now in full swing.

So far, the surveys show that public trust in and approval of Duterte have defied expectations of a reputation-bruising trial, where allegations of Duterte's unexplained wealth and wanton use of confidential fund have been heard.

Separate surveys released by Pulse Asia and Social Weather Stations (SWS) this week put Duterte's trust rating at 55% and 56%, respectively. In the Pulse Asia poll, 54% of Filipino adults also approved of her performance over the past quarter.
Pulse Asia's Ulat ng Bayan survey, conducted from September 17 to 24 through face-to-face interviews with 2,400 adults, found that 27% distrust the vice president while 19% were undecided.
On her performance, 27% disapproved and 18% could not say either way. The survey has a margin of error of ±2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
Duterte's ratings are virtually unchanged from Pulse Asia's July survey, when 58% said they trusted her and 56% approved of her work.
The only significant shift was among Class D respondents, where trust in her slipped five points to 53%.

On the other hand, the SWS survey, commissioned by Stratbase Institute, showed similarly steady numbers: 56% of Filipinos have "much trust" in Duterte, 26% have "little trust," and 17% are undecided, nearly identical to the 57%-27% split SWS recorded in June.
SWS conducted its survey from September 21 to 27.
Duterte's "much trust" rating in the SWS survey has stayed between 53% and 61% in every edition since March 2025, though it remains below the high 65% she posted in July 2024.
Mindanao bailiwick, split Luzon
Both surveys show Duterte's support remains anchored in Mindanao, her home region. Pulse Asia found 94% of Mindanawons trust her and 91% approve of her performance, with distrust at just 1%.
SWS recorded 87% "much trust" and only 4% "little trust" in the region.
Duterte also similarly holds majorities in the Visayas, with 57% trust in Pulse Asia's survey and 60% in SWS's, the latter up from 54% in June.
Luzon is more divided in perceptions of the vice president.
In Metro Manila, Pulse Asia found trust and distrust in Duterte nearly even at 43% and 41%, and her approval and disapproval tied at 42%.
In the rest of Luzon, trust stood at 37% against 38% distrust.
SWS shows Duterte has a wider edge in both areas: 46% much trust versus 33% little trust in Metro Manila, and 41% versus 35% in Balance Luzon.
Marcos underwater
The numbers stand in sharp contrast with those of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who remains well below the trust and approval ratings of Duterte.
In Pulse Asia's survey, nearly half of Filipinos disapproved of the president's performance (49%) and distrusted him (48%). Only 30% approved of his work, and 29% said they trust him.
Marcos failed to get majority approval in any geographic area or socioeconomic class, with disapproval reaching 71% in Mindanao and 66% in Class E, where it rose 14 points from July.
There were bright spots for the president in Class ABC, where his approval jumped 17 points to 37% and distrust fell 16 points. Distrust in him also eased in Mindanao, dropping 11 points to 66%.
SWS found a similar pattern, where Marcos' "much trust" rating was at 36% against 40% "little trust."
This is a slight improvement from June's 34%-45%. But it is also the fourth straight SWS survey since November 2025 in which more Filipinos expressed little trust than much trust in Marcos.
His rating has fallen from 64% in July 2024. In Mindanao, his "much trust" figure doubled from 17% in June to 35%.
Duterte's SWS trust rating has outpaced Marcos' in every survey since February 2025.
Trial backdrop
Pulse Asia's fieldwork overlapped with key developments in the impeachment trial. Throughout September, the prosecution focused on the confidential funds and unexplained wealth charge.
Earlier in the month, on September 5, Duterte was issued an arrest warrant for three counts of grave threats, charges that are also part of the impeachment case.
Duterte herself has not shown up to the impeachment trial and has not been called to take the witness stand.

The prosecution has also recently dropped its plan to call the vice president as a witness, with private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan telling reporters: "From what we heard from the defense, what she is going to say is that she knows nothing – that's all she is going to say in the witness stand."

blocks.text: The UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August despite a fall in consumer spending before chancellor John Healey’s budget.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. City economists had forecast the economy would shrink by 0.1%.

With less than a fortnight before Healey’s budget, the latest figures come as the war in the Middle East rattles the global economy and hits British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.

Against a volatile backdrop, the chancellor is under pressure to use his tax and spending address to the Commons on 28 October to announce a package of support to soften the blow. However, he will face a delicate balancing act amid a sharp increase in government borrowing costs.

In recent months, Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.

In a fillip for the chancellor, the International Monetary Fund this week upgraded its UK growth forecastsfor this year, but warned that it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.

articles.title: No timeline for lifting Land Registry paywall as ownership remains opaque
articles.summary:
Defra promised in March to work towards free access to data on large plots in England and Wales

The government has refused to say when the public will be able to freely access information…
articles.byline: Fiona Harvey, Carmen Aguilar García and Michael Goodier

blocks.text: The government has refused to say when the public will be able to freely access information about who owns large plots of land across England and Wales.
Emma Reynolds, the previous secretary of state for the environment, announced in March that the paywall protecting large amounts of the Land Registry would be partly lifted.
Campaigners called for this change in order to make large landowners more accountable, particularly for key areas such as river catchments, grouse moors and peatland.

But Reynolds did not put a date on when the paywall would be lifted, and the Land Registry is an “arm’s length body”, a non-ministerial government department that falls under the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

In setting out the land use framework in March, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) pledged only that it would “work with HM Land Registry this year to provide access to free, spatial land ownership data for larger properties covering the vast majority of England and Wales, excluding almost all homeowners”.

This may require a further public consultation, in addition to the consultation that preceded the land use framework. In July, a spokesperson for the Land Registry said: “HM Land Registry is supportive of initiatives that promote the more effective use of land. However, our plans with regard to this are still at a very early stage, and a number of aspects will be subject to consultation before any firm decisions are made. As such, we are currently unable to comment on timelines, what may be released, the format, or any associated attributes. We anticipate being in a position to provide more of an update early next year.”
In August, a Land Registry spokesperson said it was not clear which parts of the Land Registry data would be made public, nor who might be allowed to access the data and by what means.

Guy Shrubsole, the environmental campaigner and author of Who Owns England?, said: “It’s ridiculous that in the 21st century the public are kept in the dark about who owns the land beneath our feet. This is data that will help councils build more homes, expose who’s polluting our rivers and help communities restore nature.”

Andy Burnham, who took over as prime minister from Keir Starmer this summer, has made localism a key priority of his premiership. Shrubsole said allowing people to see data on the ownership of land should be part of that agenda. “Burnham has come to power promising place-first politics, and to bring unaccountable government agencies to heel,” he said. “Who owns our land underpins any politics of place, and it’s high time the Land Registry was made to reveal this profoundly important information.”

A Defra spokesperson said: “We are improving the transparency of land ownership data, and will provide free access to land ownership data for the vast majority of England, as we committed to in our land use framework. We are taking forward this commitment and will share further details as this work continues.”

articles.title: Burnham v Swinney: will the UK PM overshadow the SNP’s conference?
articles.summary:
Prime minister presents new kind of challenge for SNP, and his Scottish visit will loom large over its big event

This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party…

blocks.text: This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party conference. But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup.

Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister.

The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died.

“I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.”

Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil.

Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence. Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront.

Even among SNP voters, he is popular. Polling by PF Global found that 46% of Scots have a favourable view of Burnham, far higher than the Labour party itself, and double Keir Starmer’s when he left power. Only Swinney is more popular than the prime minister among SNP voters who supported yes in 2014, reaching a level not seen for a Labour leader since Jeremy Corbyn. Despite this, SNP figures have sought to capitalise on Burnham’s stance on the EU in their quest for a second independence vote.

“We are in a situation where Andy Burnham is actively and unilaterally opening up the conversation about whether we are able to go back to results of referendums and relitigate those decisions while saying that that same democratic principle does not apply to the people of Scotland,” said Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry. “The idea that the union can continue to exist in its current form is absolutely farcical.”

In Aberdeen, the SNP is hoping to draw a line under a bruising few years after Nicola Sturgeon’s resignation and the subsequent fraud conviction of her estranged husband and former SNP chair Peter Murrell, who is serving a five-year prison sentence for embezzling £400,000 from the party. A proceeds of crime case against Murrell is scheduled for early December.

In May, the SNP won a fifth successive election, but only enough to form a minority government in Holyrood. Despite the victory, Sturgeon criticised a “lack of vision or big picture thinking” in the campaign in the opening to her memoir. Swinney has said they were still good friends. Some SNP figures wonder how much they owe to the unpopularity of Starmer. The party also faces challenges on multiple fronts: Reform has as many MSPs as Labour in Holyrood with 17, while the Scottish Greens won a record 15 seats. The Tories have showed that they can still win seats, defeating the SNP in Aberdeen South in June.

Despite the potential for a standoff between Swinney and Burnham, there is growing appetite in Scotland for collaboration between Westminster and Holyrood. Since the May elections, there has been a sharp rise in Scots who support a closer working relationship between the UK and Scottish governments. Polling by Ipsos has found that 42% of Scots would feel happy about the SNP-led Scottish government working with London, up 12 points since Starmer was in charge in May. Just over half of Scots believe that the country is going in the wrong direction, up six points in the same time period.

This conference, the SNP has invited speakers from other separatist and pro-independence parties. Sioned Williams, deputy first minister of Wales, will give a fraternal address on Friday. Gillian Mackay, a Scottish Green party MSP, will speak at a panel about the right pathway to independence on Saturday.

“We understand, and members of the SNP know, that this is bigger than the SNP. Obviously, I fundamentally believe that the SNP will be the party who secures independence for Scotland. But that runs so much deeper throughout the Scottish population than just those who vote for the SNP. I do think that it is important at this moment to harness and to build on that support as broadly as we can,” said Bird.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Comelec did not set barangay, SK polls for December 14
articles.summary: The Comelec flags a circulating graphic as fake. Under Republic Act No. 12326, the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections are scheduled for November 13, 2028.

blocks.text: Claim: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) announced that the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) would be held on December 14, 2026.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post in the group “Duterte Legacy” that was published on October 8 carried the claim with a caption that reads, “Confirmed!”

The attached graphic mimics a Comelec announcement, displaying the poll body’s seal and the heading “Official Announcement.” It states: “This is to confirm the scheduled date for the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE). Despite any varying information, the scheduled date on record is December 14, 2026.”
Its text further states: “PAALALA: Ang opisyal na petsa ay maaaring magbago ayon sa batas. Manatiling nakatutok para sa anumang opisyal na bagong anunsyo mula sa COMELEC.”
(Reminder: The official date may change according to law. Stay tuned for any official new announcement from the Comelec.)
As of writing, the post had drawn 763 reactions, 136 comments, and 140 shares.

The facts: The Comelec did not announce a December 14 BSKE. On October 10, it warned the public that the circulating graphic was fake and urged the public to rely on the poll body’s official website and social media accounts for election-related announcements.

The graphic cites no law or Comelec resolution establishing December 14 as the election date. It provides no resolution number and merely directs readers to the Comelec website. The use of the poll body’s seal and official-looking design does not establish its authenticity.

Under Republic Act (RA) No. 12326, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on September 24, the next BSKE is scheduled for November 13, 2028. The law postponed the elections from the previous schedule of November 2, 2026.

Petitions before the Supreme Court seek to block the new law and compel the Comelec to hold the elections in 2026. The poll body has said that RA 12326 remains in effect because the Court has not issued a temporary restraining order.

Date change: The BSKE was initially scheduled for December 1, 2025. In August 2025, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed RA 12232, postponing the elections to November 2, 2026, and setting a four-year term for barangay and SK officials.
Senator Francis Escudero then filed Senate Bill No. 2387 in August 2026, seeking to extend the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years, amending RA 12232.

Escudero’s proposed measure was subsequently enacted as RA 12326. The law provides for elections every five years, on the second Monday of November, beginning in 2028. (READ: How often have barangay, SK elections been postponed?)

Fake dates: The shifting election schedules have fueled misinformation online. Rappler previously fact-checked a claim that the postponement had already become law before Marcos signed it, as well as another claiming that the elections would be held this coming November 28. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar, who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies from the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship for 2024.

articles.title: Microsoft, partners disrupt phishing kit ecosystem behind cybercrime operations
articles.summary: Microsoft and its partners dismantle three parts of a wide-ranging cybercrime marketplace: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man

blocks.text: Microsoft and its partners dismantle three parts of a wide-ranging cybercrime marketplace: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man

items: Microsoft collaborated with Japan's National Police Agency and partners to dismantle a Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace responsible for phishing kits.
The operation targeted three components of the marketplace: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man, which collectively enabled over one billion malicious messages aimed at various organizations worldwide.
The phishing kits allowed criminals to impersonate trusted organizations, making it easier to execute phishing attacks across multiple sectors and countries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Microsoft worked with Japan’s National Police Agency and a host of partners, including cybersecurity companies and global nonprofit organization Health-ISAC, to dismantle part of the operations of a Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace responsible for creating and selling phishing kits — or accounts, hosting services and tools for building fake websites and online identities.
In an October 14 blog post, Microsoft said it and Health-ISAC dismantled three parts of that marketplace’s infrastructure: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man.

Steven Masada, general counsel and general manager of Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, said YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have since January 2026 “collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone.”

He added, “These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators.”

While YAM Store provided the infrastructure, the phishing kits sold on the marketplace, including CoGUI and Iron Man, provided bad actors with access to ready-made templates allowing them to impersonate trusted organizations. With the templates in hand, criminals could quickly send email, text and web content tailored to specific brands, industries, and countries in an effort to get people to click on phishing links.

Masada explained that the phishing kits allowed for impersonation attempts across a spectrum of organizations, from government agencies to banks, retailers, and parcel delivery services from various countries and in numerous languages.

Masada added, “YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on.”
A more technical breakdown of the phishing infrastructure that complements the Microsoft blogpost is available on Microsoft’s security blog. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Filipinos rank among top 3 AI users on messaging platform
articles.summary: Filipinos rank among the top three markets worldwide for artificial intelligence feature usage on Rakuten Viber, according to the messaging platform, with young professionals among the most active…

blocks.text: Filipinos rank among the top three markets worldwide for artificial intelligence feature usage on Rakuten Viber, according to the messaging platform, with young professionals among the most active users of its AI tools.

Viber Chief Product Officer Nadav Melnick said nearly 20% of the platform’s monthly active AI users in the Philippines are aged 25 to 34, followed closely by users aged 35 to 44. The company said the figures reflect growing use of AI for everyday tasks, including finding information, translating messages, summarizing conversations, and drafting replies.

Almost half of AI interactions among Filipino users take place through Viber’s dedicated ChatGPT Tab, where users can ask questions, brainstorm ideas, and seek assistance with daily activities. The Translate feature is another popular tool, alongside Your News, Unread Recap, and AI Reply.

“The strongest adoption is among young professionals and active communicators. These are people balancing work, side hustles, and personal lives,” Melnick said. He added that users were turning to AI because the tools could save time in their daily routines.
AI adoption brings privacy questions

As AI becomes more accessible through messaging apps, the information users share with these tools remains an important consideration. Messages can contain personal details, workplace information, financial records, and other sensitive material that users may not intend to share beyond a conversation.

Viber Chief Revenue Officer Cristina Constandache said the company applies its privacy and security principles to its AI integration, including its partnership with OpenAI to bring ChatGPT services to the platform.
Constandache said Viber does not use users’ data to train AI models and that users retain control over whether and how they access its AI features.
“On Viber, AI is never reading user messages passively in the background,” Constandache said, adding that users decide whether to use AI and how much of their data they share with it.

These assurances are relevant as users become accustomed to asking AI tools to process information or generate responses. However, users should still understand what information they submit to an AI feature and how that feature handles it, particularly when working with confidential or sensitive material.

Viber’s Philippine market research, conducted by JTN Research, found that 41% of Filipinos regularly use the platform for work chats, while 46% use it to connect with businesses. The figures underscore the range of personal and professional communications taking place on messaging platforms.
Philippines remains a key market

AI adoption is part of a broader pattern of engagement with Viber in the Philippines. Senior Director for Asia-Pacific David Tse said Filipino users spend more time on the app daily than users in other markets, while the company forecasts 16.5% growth in monthly active users in the country.

The Philippines also leads Viber’s markets in several paid and business services. The company reported a 34.3% increase in local ViberPlus subscribers and a 75.5% growth in Philippine contributions to ViberPlus global revenue.

Viber Dating’s average monthly active users in the country grew by 96.9%, compared with a global average of 44%, according to the company. Filipino users also account for 56% of new profiles on the service.

Businesses are another part of the platform’s local growth. The Philippines accounts for 24% of Viber’s global live business accounts, with the company reporting a 20.5% increase in live accounts and 127.3% growth in meaningful business interactions.

Viber also plans to work with the Department of Tourism to help travelers discover accredited tourism businesses through Viber Business Accounts and Marketplace. The proposed partnership aims to give tourism-related micro, small, and medium enterprises another way to reach customers while helping visitors find legitimate businesses.

The company’s growing range of services reflects how messaging platforms are expanding beyond personal communication. As AI features become part of that ecosystem, their usefulness will depend not only on how easily people can access them, but also on whether users understand their capabilities and the privacy considerations involved in using them

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Thanks to an erratic Trump, peace in Ukraine is still far away
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As Russia resists a ceasefire and Trump’s shifting priorities unsettle allies, an end to the conflict isn’t getting any closer

Good morning. In his usual…

blocks.text: Good morning. In his usual asinine unconventional approach to international relations, Donald Trump announced on Sunday (via Truth Social, how else) an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”, apparently without checking with either side. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said any such deal was “news to me,” nonetheless declared he was “ready and we will accept it”. Vladimir Putin responded by blowing up some Ukrainian power plants.

This has been the tenor of much diplomacy during Trump’s tenure: false starts, U-turns, incoherent positions (and some playful flirting with Vlad). Meanwhile fighting continues, and America’s allies attempt to manage the fallout. Andy Burnham hosted Zelenskyy at Downing Street yesterday, stating the UK is doubling down on its support for Ukraine, and pointedly calling on others to “follow suit”.

It’s a negotiators nightmare. So how are ambassadors, spooks and diplomats handling the chaos? Is an actual ceasefire or peace deal within their grasp? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to career diplomat and former ambassador Nigel Gould-Davies to find out. Before that, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK | Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
Gaza | Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.
EU | Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.

Ukraine | Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to immediately halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry.
Vaccine | Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests’

blocks.caption: Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian strike on a residential building in Kharkiv. Photograph: Sergey Kozlov/EPA

blocks.text: Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, efforts to secure either a temporary ceasefire or a permanent peace deal have resolutely failed. Endless rounds of talks in Belarus, Turkey, Abu Dhabi and Geneva have all proved futile. To Nigel Gould-Davies, it’s obvious why. A former British diplomat, he was head of economics at the Foreign Office in Moscow before his stint as the UK’s ambassador to Belarus. Today, he is senior fellow for Russia and Eurasia at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

Gould-Davies tells me that there are established norms for negotiating during military conflicts. Diplomats look for the interests, needs and red lines that each side articulates, in pursuit of the elusive “win set”.

“A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests to end the fighting than to continue,” he says. “You have to find that overlap in the Venn diagram that leads to a defined set of conditions which, despite involving painful compromises, is ultimately judged to better serve each side than continuing to fight.
“The problem with this situation is that Russia has no interest in ending the war,” he says. Tricky to find common ground, then.

It is through this lens that we should view all Russia-Ukraine talks since Trump’s return to the presidency, Gould-Davies suggests. “They have not really been negotiations,” but “parallel efforts by Russia and Ukraine to persuade the White House it’s the other side’s fault” that a peace agreement (and, perhaps more importantly to Trump, that elusive Nobel peace prize) had failed to materialise.

That said, the respective red lines aren’t difficult to identify. Ukraine has time and again said it is willing to accept an unconditional ceasefire. “Russia, by contrast, has repeatedly said publicly that it is not interested in a ceasefire,” says Gould-Davies, only in a full and final end to the war that, in Russian terms, means “decisive superiority and dominance over a severely weakened Ukraine”.
That’s an outcome Ukraine can’t, and won’t, sign up for.
The ‘non-standard president’

This is already a headache for UK, European and American diplomats, who most recently met in Miami at the end of last week. But there’s also the added Trump-shaped impediment to grapple with; what Gould-Davies diplomatically describes as the challenge of having “a non-standard president” in the White House. When Trump unilaterally declared an energy ceasefire, Gould-Davies says, it had “no basis whatsoever in reality”. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv was aware. “He simply made it up … a product of a fantasy.”

The botched digital diplomacy aside, Trump’s interests also don’t appear aligned with Ukraine or traditional US allies. “[Trump’s] natural centre of gravity is to favour Russia,” says Gould-Davies, citing restrictions on US weapons supplies and past pauses in intelligence sharing. Yesterday, Zelenskyy accused Trump of restricting Ukrainian access to “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences.

Granted, Trump has at times sided with the Ukrainian president: sanctioning Russian oil companies and helping Ukraine target Russian energy infrastructure. But for all Trump’s “lurching”, says Gould-Davies, his theory of ending the war involves concessions to Russia and coercion of Ukraine.
The price of a deal

After a period of relative quiet from Trump on the Russia-Ukraine front, this week Trump’s attention returned. With Americans facing soaring energy costs, he announced a plan to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down pump prices, much to the dismay not just of European leaders but a bipartisan group of US senators, too.

Leave aside, for a second, suggestions that these imports could be illegal under American law and that quantities being discussed are seemingly too small to actually affect prices, even if the fuel could reach the US ahead of next month’s midterms, as Trump hopes.

In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal “is only the visible tip of the iceberg”, says Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a “much more substantial” pro-Russia tilt.

Gould-Davies suspects that Trump could be, via Russia, seeking to get Iran to ease the blockade on the strait of Hormuz, in the hope of actually bringing down fuel prices before American voters head to the polls. Putin’s quid pro quo for brokering these efforts, Gould-Davies says, “could be an easing of America’s sanctions on Russia and an ending to America’s support for Ukraine”.
It’s just a theory, he caveats, “but join the dots and it logically makes sense”.
Either way, for diplomats it’s just further proof that Trump’s mercurial methods are more a hindrance than help.
The quiet work behind the scenes

Nonetheless, diplomatic back channels remain operational: secret, closed-door meetings and off-the-record communications between all sides. Not that Gould-Davies thinks they’re worth the effort. “There is a degree of collective delusion here,” he says: “A hope that Russia can somehow be persuaded” to change course, for which “there is literally no evidence for that whatsoever”. He worries that these informal discussions could even be “actively unhelpful, because they perpetuate the illusion that peace may be around the corner”.

And, while Europe might traditionally have focused its diplomatic efforts in hostile territory, attention has now turned towards the US itself. There’s still hope that Trump’s whispers might pay further dividends. As Gould-Davies puts it, this “Avengers assemble” approach has seen European leaders and diplomats descend on Washington when Trump’s veered too far off course. For all the tumult, he says, this has proved effective in averting “the nightmare scenario” of Trump binning off America’s old transatlantic partners for good.

But as fans of Netflix’s The Diplomat will know, even diplomacy between allies isn’t plain sailing. “Right now even ‘the White House’ is an abstraction,” says Gould-Davies. “It consists of many different players, plenty of whom have different views privately from President Trump.” Take John Ratcliffe, director of the CIA, who visited Moscow this summer. There is “reliable speculation”, says Gould-Davies, that he hoped to “warn Russia against escalation into Europe”. It’s a totally different note to those currently being struck by Trump.

“There are people in positions of power and influence still in this administration who understand the problem of Russia in the right way,” says Gould-Davies. With that in mind, western diplomats will continue to try to shift the balance of influences within the White House, but they’re reliant on what he labels a White House Kremlinology – “trying to understand the different views and moods of those around Trump and who will be the last person to whisper in his ear.”

blocks.text: India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown

A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims that it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters. But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that the country is sliding further into autocracy. blocks.caption: Hive of activity … Aref Haboo (left), Bybi’s principal beekeeper, with Mohamed, a fellow apiarist. Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Copenhagen’s rooftops live 80 to 100 colonies of honeybees, tended by a collective of beekeepers called Bybi.
Set up in 2010 with the aim of employing marginalised people, Bybi’s work has evolved into a response to the modern economic system.

With the help of volunteers, from refugees to people on incapacity benefits, they produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year, which they sell (often letting people pay what they like) or give away, asking that people share it with loved ones and plant a flower to help the bees. They also run schools programmes, supported by sponsorships from universities and corporations.
“Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection,” says founder Oliver Maxwell, “asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?”

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly asked celebrity chaser friend if he could post phone to her in WA to throw in water, court told
articles.summary: Stacey Parker was contacted following alleged murders, years after meeting Lamarre-Condon in Sydney and bonding over scepticism of Covid vaccines

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon asked a friend in Western Australia if he could post her a phone to be thrown into a body of water, and told her he’d been “set up” over the disappearance of two men, a court has heard.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon’s friend Stacey Parker, who lives in WA, told the NSW supreme court on Thursday that she first met the police officer in 2010.

The two were celebrity hunting for American rapper Pitbull outside the Channel 7 studios while Sunrise was being filmed. They exchanged numbers to try to double their chances of encountering the celebrity and continued to speak and meet whenever she travelled to Sydney in the following years.
Asked if they had any shared interests beyond celebrity chasing, Parker said they would speak about the Covid pandemic.
She told the jury she “didn’t agree with the injections and whatnot” and explained she would go to protests.
Knowing Lamarre-Condon was a police officer, she asked him how he could “stand there and push back against people fighting for freedom”.
“He just told me it was devil’s work,” she told the court.

Lamarre-Condon on 12 February 2024 asked if they could switch to messaging on the encrypted messaging app Signal, the court heard. On 20 February 2024, a day after the alleged murders, he called her and asked if she could do him a favour.
“He told me that he’d stolen some police files from the commissioner to do with Covid and he’d wanted me to get rid of a phone,” Parker told the court.
“He wanted me to turn the phone on, turn it off and throw it into some body of water. I was going to do it not knowing what it was.”

blocks.caption: A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP

blocks.text: Lamarre-Condon specifically asked her to turn it on for about 10 minutes so it could “ping” and then turn it back off before disposing of it 30km to 40km from her home, Parker told the court.
Two days later, he called her again and said police had been searching for him, she told the court on Thursday.
“He’s said that the detectives had been at his mum’s place.
“[He said] he had been set up for two guys missing in Sydney and he used to know one of them. He asked me again what I had to do with the phone so I told him what I was going to do.”
Unlike the earlier call, where the officer seemed “very easy to talk to”, Parker said his tone in the later discussion felt like “he wanted to hear from me that I knew what I had to do”.
Soon after, a friend sent her a news article that said Baird and Davies had disappeared and Lamarre-Condon was wanted for questioning.

“I started reading through the article and it said that Jesse’s phone had sent messages to his friends saying he was going on a road trip to Perth,” she told the court. The friend never received a package from Lamarre-Condon.

Earlier on Thursday, she told the court she had seen the policeman post a photo with socialite Kourtney Kardashian and Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker and hoped Lamarre-Condon could get her close to a country singer she liked.
She sent him a message on 16 February 2024 that stated: “If you can get to Kourt Kardashian, then surely you can get us to Lainey Wilson.”

blocks.caption: Artwork for a 2024 memorial for Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird. Photograph: Nordacious

blocks.text: Final messages from phone
Prosecutors on Thursday also read out a statement from Baird’s friend and former colleague Jemma Barge about the last messages she received from his phone.
The night before he was killed, Baird sent her a message wishing her well before she began a new job.
“It’s Sunday night, which means one big thing: Jem’s big day tomorrow, ahh,” the text read to the court states. “Good luck bear, you will smash it like you do everything else.”
On Monday, she responded to the message, told him about her first day in the new role and asked if he would be free to catch up the following week, the jury was told.

According to her statement, a final message from Baird’s phone – sent the day after he was killed – said: “I’m so happy for you bear, I might be going to Perth but if I don’t end up going, then I’ll definitely let you know.”
Barge later read the news that Baird and Davies were missing. While watching a press conference she couldn’t stop thinking about the last message she received from Baird’s phone, the court was told.
“I was under the impression something had already occurred before this text message had been sent to me,” she said in her statement.
The defence team has claimed Baird and Davies were accidentally shot in two separate struggles with the accused while he acted in “self-defence”.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

blocks.text: KEY POST. Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos leads the floor after being elected House majority leader on July 28, 2025.
Sandro Marcos' Facebook
The congressman's office has kept the move low-key, providing no press release or photo handout of the oath taking

MANILA, Philippines – House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos has left Partido Federal, the party of his father President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and joined Lakas CMD, the party of his uncle and mentor, former speaker Martin Romualdez.
A source told Rappler that the younger Marcos took his oath before Lakas member and Camiguin Representative JJ Romualdo at the House of Representatives on Monday, October 11.

Marcos’ office has kept the move low-key, providing no press release or photo handout of the oath taking. Former president and Pampanga 2nd District Representative Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, however, was said to be present at the event.

No reason has been given for his party transfer, which comes weeks after its president Romualdez was arrested for plunder in connection with the flood control and overall national budget corruption scandal.
The party hasn’t distanced itself from Romualdez despite the controversy, and repeated calls for impartiality and due process after his arrest.
Lakas remains the biggest contingent in the House, with around 60 members, although its numbers are down from its peak of more than 100 members in the 19th Congress.
The lower chamber’s second largest delegation, National Unity Party, isn’t far behind, with around 50 members.
Rappler has reached out to both Lakas and PFP for comment, but they have yet to respond. – Rappler.com

articles.title: MIDEA kicks off Xpress Hub tour with space and money saving appliances
articles.summary: Written by INQUIRER.net Tech Editor Jayvee Fernandez for Midea As a southie, I really make it a point to make my trips up north worth the drive. After discovering the MIDEA Xpress Hub was unveiling…

blocks.text: Written by INQUIRER.net Tech Editor Jayvee Fernandez for Midea

As a southie, I really make it a point to make my trips up north worth the drive. After discovering the MIDEA Xpress Hub was unveiling its new product line at Waltermart in North EDSA, I had to see for myself what new things MIDEA had to unveil. I say this as a MIDEA customer, having two aircons, and one smart refrigerator installed just last year.

One thing I learned is that MIDEA is quite deliberate with their product releases. I’ve seen their booths at IFA in Berlin for two consecutive years. On one end, they’ve focused on AI and the smart home – my refrigerator notifies me if the kids leave the door open! But this time, the Xpress Hub had other things to offer. In this economy, many families are on save mode. It doesn’t necessarily mean they are consuming less — it has more to do with making smarter decisions to save where it counts. There were three products I found super interesting: a low-smoke griddle, the XpressFlame gas range, and the fully electric stovetop range and oven.
Incremental gains, bigger savings

Consider the Midea XpressFlame gas range. Midea engineered an advanced burner system that is 10% more efficient than standard burners. On paper, 10% looks like a modest, incremental saving, but when that adds up, it becomes equivalent to saving one tank of gas per year. That’s pretty huge given the price of gas and oil in this economy.

The XpressFlame achieves the saving with the way the burner is designed. The heat is released in a vortex-like flame with wider slits that is more akin to Asian cooking. Apparently most gas ranges are designed for the western market and the wider slits work better for cooking things like fried rice, stir fry, and other Asian dishes.
Indoor grilling reimagined

Then there is the Midea Low-Smoke Griddle. Indoor grilling is historically a compromise. If you want that deep, high-heat sear on a piece of meat, you usually have to accept the inevitable tax: a smoke-filled living room, greasy residue settling on your furniture, and your clothes smelling like a barbecue joint for the next twelve hours. In an enclosed home, that smell will last the entire evening till the next morning.

This griddle tackles those pain points through two specific engineering choices. First, it uses graphene infrared heating that reaches cooking temperature in a mere 0.2 seconds. There is no tedious pre-heating cycle where energy is wasted heating up an empty plate. Second, the built-in Smoke Guard technology directs oils and drippings away from the heating elements before they can burn and vaporize into blue smoke. The entire bottom is a catch basin that you need to fill with water. This is where the oils dissipate so smoke doesn’t rise and it also acts as a secondary heating element from the bottom of the grill.

To be clear, this product is built for the urban professional living in a tightly sealed condo who wants a steak on a Tuesday evening without triggering the building’s smoke alarms. It’s meant for the family that wants a simple and fun way to grill at the dinner table without the hassles of smoking and charring.
The premium of floor space

The third piece of the puzzle is the Midea 50cm All-Electric Range. If you live in a suburban home with a massive open-concept kitchen, appliance dimensions rarely cross your mind. But for those navigating dense city apartments, space is the ultimate luxury.

A 50cm footprint means you are reclaiming valuable physical territory in your kitchen layout. Instead of relying on a mismatched array of single-burner portable stoves cluttering your countertops, this range consolidates four independent ceramic cooking zones and a spacious oven into a single, compact profile. The smooth ceramic glass surface also removes the physical dread of cleanup—a quick wipe down replaces the tedious scrub-and-soak routine required by traditional iron grates.
If you’re an aspiring home baker, the precision oven allows you to bake pastries that are more sensitive to temperature.
As an added bonus, if you’re running off-grid power like solar panels, your electricity costs for cooking can actually be zero!
Pragmatism over hype

Seeing these releases made me realize that while high-concept smart home concepts make for great press releases at European trade shows, pragmatic, localized engineering is what actually makes the daily quality of life in a Filipino home simply ideal.
Whether it is reclaiming an extra month of cooking gas or grilling indoors without the lingering odor of smoke, it’s all about the way tech works for you and for your home.
The Midea Xpress Hub tour will be making its next destination this coming October 29 to November 2 at Abenson Waltermart Sucat Road.

articles.title: ‘Manosphere’ podcasts and moon-landing conspiracy theories to remain online under new laws, Wells says
articles.summary:
Communications minister rebuts claims that Labor’s digital duty of care laws would lead to government control of speech

  • Follow our

blocks.text: Australians could still “listen to manosphere podcasts” or “say the moon landing was fake” under proposed new online safety laws, Anika Wells has stressed as she rubbished claims they would lead to government censorship

The communications minister also said she was considering updates to the digital duty of care laws to allow individual Australians to directly sue big tech companies flouting the new rules. This has been a key demand from the Greens for their support for the laws, while the Coalition accuses Labor of plans to “secretly control Australian speech”.

“This is not about what people say on the internet,” Wells told the National Press Club on Thursday. “It’s about what platforms do on the internet, and your right to disagree with me or the government or believe whatever you want to believe will not be impinged by a digital duty of care.
“Your right to be free from harm, hopefully, will be improved.”

Wells said that “if adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction”.
“We are not controlling free speech, and we are not conducting covert surveillance,” Wells said.

The digital duty of care laws, introduced into parliament on Thursday after months of discussion and consultation, would add several planks to Australia’s online safety regime. The government said it would place “an overarching obligation” for tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians”, and replacing an existing range of online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content.

Wells has suggested misogynistic, pro-terror, suicide and self-harm, or eating disorder content would be captured by the laws, which will apply to platforms such as social media, online games, apps and chatbots.
“If you build it, you are responsible for its risks,” Wells said, likening the reforms to having seatbelts in cars.

blocks.caption: Digital duty laws still allow manosphere content and conspiracy theories, says Wells – video

blocks.text: “We must shift the burden from the shoulders of victims to the companies that are creating the environments where harms occur.”

The changes also provide for what the government has dubbed “my feed my way”, allowing social media users to opt-out of algorithmic content feeds and instead see content only from pages they have actively chosen to follow. Platforms face fines of more than $100m for non-compliance.

But the reforms have been met with ferocious opposition from conservative campaign groups and politicians, who have claimed the ability to class content as “harmful” would create a framework for government censorship.

The issue was a key talking point at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) conference in Brisbane over the weekend. The campaign group, Advance, has dubbed it a “Big Brother bill”, likening it to Labor’s dumped misinformation bill and collecting nearly 75,000 signatures on a petition calling for it to be scrapped.

Liberal frontbencher James Paterson claimed the bill was a bid “to secretly control Australian speech, to censor Australian speech”. The shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, said the Coalition was vehemently opposed to the bill.

One key criticism is the ability of regulators and researchers to create so-called “sockpuppets”, or pseudonymous accounts on various networks, which the government argues is critical to test how platforms are complying with legislation.
after newsletter promotion

But rightwing media personalities, podcasters and politicians have railed against this provision. Pauline Hanson claimed it would lead to “swarms of AI-powered government bots to feed you propaganda and record what you do online”.

Wells dismissed these suggestions, saying “sockpuppets” would only be used for research and enforcement purposes. The eSafety commissioner must report annually on its use of sockpuppets, and such accounts can engage with other users of an online service “only to the extent necessary to prevent closure of an account”.

Wells said: “The idea that any capacity would be spent as an independent regulator trying to spread government propaganda, rather than trying to shut down pro-terror content going to 13-year-old boys in Western Sydney or eating disorder content going to 14-year-old girls in Western Australia, is not a tenable argument.”
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young claimed the campaigns against the legislation were “running cover for big tech”.

“To suggest this is about censorship or about shutting down anything is absolute rubbish. It is a fake debate, it’s got nothing to do with it, and it is purely the radical right running the speaking points of big tech,” she said.

The Greens are broadly supportive of the bill, but want Labor to strengthen rules, including adding the ability for ordinary Australians to take private action against tech companies for breaches, and for fines to be dramatically increased.
Wells said it was “something we would contemplate”, noting such schemes had been successful in the United States. But she also urged the Coalition to reopen negotiations.
The bill will be go to a Senate inquiry, to report back in late November. Labor hopes to pass it this year.

articles.title: Zaldy Co aide: I turned down P15M offer to recant allegations vs Romualdez
articles.summary: Zaldy Co aide: I turned down P15M offer to recant allegations vs Romualdez

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 1:12pm
Zaldy Co's former aide said Thursday that he turned down millions of pesos being offered to him to recant his allegations against former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez.
Rodante Orbillo, a witness for the prosecution, made the testimony during Day 3 of the bail hearing of Romualdez, who is in detention due to a P7.4 billion plunder case.
“P15 million pataas,” Orbillo said when asked by Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Ronald Moreno how much the money offer was.
(P15M and higher.)
Orbillo later said the offer even reached as high as P20 million and that there was also a case of P8 million.
Asked by Moreno why he turned down the offer of money, Orbillo said he needs to stand for the truth since he was previously falsely accused of frustrated murder in the past.

“Ito na lang po ang totoong nangyari sa buhay ko, iyong trabaho kay Cong Zaldy Co. Kaya hindi niya ako nakumbinsi,” Orbillo said, referring to Benny Bulontante, one of the accusers of Romualdez who later recanted.
(This is the only thing that remains real in my life —my work with Cong. Zaldy Co. That is why he couldn’t convince me.)
Orbillo said that Bulontante accepted the offer of money to recant, but he could not say how much it was.
'Maleta'

Asked by the prosecution panel how he was able to ascertain that it was the house of Romualdez in 14 Narra in Forbes Park, Orbillo said it is because he saw Romualdez’s personal driver, Bobby, in the said house.
“Nasa maleta po, bundled na. Maamoy niyo po iyong bagong pera. Nasusuya na nga po ako [sa amoy].” Orbillo said of cash deliveries to Romualdez.
(The money was in suitcases. You can smell the scent of newly printed money.)
“Bago po dalhin kay Cong Martin, bibilangin po muna [sa bahay ni Zaldy Co],” Orbillo added.
(Before bringing them to Cong Martin, we count the money in Zaldy Co’s house.)
Orbillo also testified he delivered money to Romualdez in three other locations.
Likewise, Orbillo said that he delivered alleged kickbacks to Senator Vicente Sotto III, former Marikina Rep. Stella Quimbo and former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV from 2022 to 2024.
Trillanes was a Senator from 2007 to 2016. But he was not a senator in 2022 as he lost during the elections.
Sotto was also not a Senator from 2022 to 2025, which covers the years Co served as House appropriations chair.
Quimbo, meanwhile, served as House appropriations panel chair senior vice chair from 2022 to 2024.
GMA News Online is still seeking comment from incumbent and former lawmakers in connection with Orbillo’s allegations. —VAL, GMA News
